issues.legal_issue: The prohibition on enforcing rights in property held benami does not bar a suit instituted before that prohibition applies.
material_facts: The suit sought a declaration of ownership based on the claim that the conveyance in another person's name was security for a loan rather than a transfer of beneficial ownership.
The suit was instituted before the relevant prohibition came into force.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, although that conclusion did not determine whether the claimant had proved the merits of the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 is not retrospective and does not bar suits instituted before it came into force. The Court applied R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, (1995) 2 SCC 630, which overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare, (1989) 2 SCC 95, on retrospectivity.

predicates.benami_ownership_suit: The claimant brought a suit asserting beneficial ownership of property conveyed in another person's name.
predicates.suit_filed_before_claim_prohibition_appl: The claimant instituted the suit before the restriction on enforcing such claims applied.

issues.definition: When a beneficial-ownership suit concerns property conveyed in another person's name and was instituted before the restriction applied, the claim is not barred by that restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may set aside factual findings that are perverse and, in substance, based on no evidence without impermissibly rehearing the case as a first appellate court.
material_facts: The dispute reached the High Court in a second appeal, in which questions of law had been framed.
The first appellate court had decreed the claimant's suit, but the High Court found that its conclusions were unsupported by evidence and perverse.
The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court and rejected the contention that it had reappreciated the evidence as a first appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court did not exceed its second appellate jurisdiction; it correctly interfered because the first appellate decision was perverse and based on no evidence.
issues.legal_principle: In a second appeal, interference with factual findings is not an impermissible reappraisal where the findings are perverse and, in substance, rest on no evidence. The Court applied that distinction in rejecting the challenge to the High Court's approach.

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision was made in a second appeal from a first appellate judgment.
predicates.first_appellate_finding_perverse_or_with: The first appellate court's factual conclusion was perverse or had no evidentiary basis.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, a perverse or evidentially unsupported first appellate finding may be set aside without treating the proceeding as a fresh first appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant's ownership and possession claims may fail when the claimant does not prove them and does not examine a vital witness without explanation.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that the conveyance in another person's name was only security for a loan and sought declarations of ownership and an injunction protecting possession.
The claimant did not establish title or possession to the High Court's satisfaction.
The claimant did not call the claimant's brother, whose evidence was central to the alleged transaction and the dispute over possession, and offered no explanation for that omission.
The Supreme Court agreed that the omission justified an adverse inference and that the first appellate decree was based on no evidence.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish entitlement to the declaration and injunction, and the first appellate decree in the claimant's favour could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: A court may draw an adverse inference when a party fails without explanation to examine a witness whose evidence is vital to the party's case. The Court treated the missing testimony, together with the failure to prove title and possession, as supporting the conclusion that the claim lacked an evidentiary basis.

predicates.ownership_and_possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking recognition of ownership and protection of possession.
predicates.title_or_possession_not_proved: The claimant's evidence did not establish title or possession of the property.
predicates.material_witness_not_examined_without_ex: The claimant did not examine a witness whose evidence was central to the claim and gave no explanation for that omission.

issues.definition: An ownership and possession claim fails when the claimant does not prove title or possession and leaves a central witness unexamined without explanation.

issues.legal_issue: Exemplary costs are warranted when litigation is used to obstruct enforcement of a final court order and prolongs the successful party's inability to obtain its benefit.
material_facts: An eviction order had become final, but execution to recover possession remained pending.
During execution, a relative of the person subject to eviction brought a suit asserting ownership and obtained an ex parte injunction.
The suit followed the failure of the person subject to eviction to establish the same essential claim in the eviction proceedings and delayed recovery of possession for many years.
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and imposed costs payable to the party entitled to possession.
issues.conclusion: The Court imposed exemplary costs on the appellant for litigation that delayed enforcement of the final eviction order.
issues.legal_principle: Courts should take serious note of attempts to circumvent court orders through dubious or obstructive litigation and may impose exemplary costs to curb that conduct. The Court relied on the circumstances and prolonged obstruction in this case; it cited no specific provision or earlier case for the costs ruling.

predicates.execution_obstruction_suit: A litigant brought a separate suit while enforcement of a final court order was underway, seeking relief that obstructed that enforcement.
predicates.final_court_order_delayed_by_litigation: The separate litigation prolonged the successful party's inability to obtain the benefit of the final order.

issues.definition: When a separate suit obstructs execution and prolongs the denial of the benefit of a final order, exemplary costs may be imposed.
